question: Is it permissible to wipe over ordinary cloth socks in wudu instead of washing the feet?
asked: I pray dhuhr at my workplace every single day, and I feel uncomfortable washing my feet in the sink, for obvious reasons. I know there's a controversy over masah, or wiping over the socks. Can you please explain to us and give us your position on wiping over the socks?
answer:
So this is the simple question: masah over the socks. Not over the shoe, or over the khuff, or the leather.

So realize, dear brother in Islam, and all of us benefit from this, brothers and sisters, because the rulings apply to both men and women. There's no difference of opinion between men and women when it comes to wiping over the socks; exactly the same that applies to men applies to women.

Realize that wiping over a full covering that is impermeable to water, which is leather or something of that nature, wiping over a full covering of the foot that covers the ankles and is impermeable, is unanimously accepted by all of the scholars of Islam, or I should say all of the scholars of Sunni Islam. So much so that it became a point of theology. You find this in 'Aqidah Tahawiyyah: that Sunni Muslims believe it is permissible to wipe over the khuff, which is the leather sock. Why? Because the other, non-Sunni group said this thing is not permissible. The famous non-Sunni group, there's only one famous non-Sunni group; when I say non-Sunni, there's one group you should think of. It says you're not allowed to wipe over the sock. And the Khawarij said you cannot wipe over the socks, and others said you cannot wipe over... sorry, not the sock, the leather sock, let's say.

So it became a point of theology, because so many ahadith mention the Prophet ﷺ wiping over the leather sock, which is the khuff in Arabic. So all the madhhabs agree, and this is something you will find no controversy over: that if you're wearing a covering that covers the ankle and that is impermeable to water, which is leather for example, or anything impermeable to water, right, and you have wudu, and you put your feet into this shoe, or this leather sock, in the state of wudu, then you may do masah one day when you're not traveling and three days if you are traveling. This is unanimous; no ikhtilaf.

But who wears leather socks in our times? Nobody. So the ikhtilaf comes over what issue? This is why I want you to be clear here: the controversy is over socks that are permeable. That's the controversy. It's not over masah. Some people don't understand; they say, "Oh, there's a controversy of masah." No, there is no controversy over masah, zero. It is by unanimous consensus allowed.

And even the Qur'an references the permissibility of masah, in Surah al-Ma'idah, verse 6, the famous one. It's a bit advanced, but basically, wa arjulakum versus wa arjulikum: you can explicitly derive masah from the verse in the Qur'an. "Wipe over your feet" is the verse in the Qur'an, and it can also be read "wash over your feet" in the qira'at of the Qur'an. So the point is, it is very, very explicit.

Now, as for the hadith of the Prophet, it is mutawatir. Over 20 sahabah reported masah over khuff, and that's why there is no controversy, as we said, in Sunni Islam. The most famous hadith, which you should all be aware of, is the hadith of Jarir ibn Abdullah al-Bajali: that Jarir ibn Abdullah went to the bathroom, relieved himself, came back, and he wiped over the sock. His students said, "How can you wipe over the sock?" And he said, "Why shouldn't I? I saw the Prophet ﷺ use the restroom, come back, and then wipe over his sock."

In another version, the Sahabi said: I came down to take the sock, the shoe (when I say sock, right now think of leather sock), to take the khuff off from the Prophet, and he said to me, "Leave it on, for I wore them when I was in the state of wudu." And I saw him wipe over the khuff. Right, wipe over the khuff. And there are many, many narrations in this regard.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, the famous shaykh of Abu Hanifa, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, the greatest scholar of Kufa of the students of the sahabah, said: we would love this hadith of Jarir ibn Abdullah, because Jarir accepted Islam after Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed. Now, what has it got to do with anything? Surah al-Ma'idah is the surah in which Allah talks about wudu: "O you who believe, when you stand up to pray, then wash your face and wipe your head and wash your hands and your feet." This ayah is in Surah al-which one? Al-Ma'idah. Jarir accepted Islam after al-Ma'idah, and Jarir is saying: I saw with my own eyes, after this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ did what? Wipe over the socks, the leather sock. And so al-Nakha'i is saying, we all loved this hadith because we can use it to refute those who say wiping is abrogated. It's not abrogated: the Qur'an came, and the Prophet ﷺ is still wiping over the sock.

So we have all of this, and that's what Imam al-Nawawi says: there is ijma' of anyone whose ijma' we care about that it is allowed to wipe over the khuff, whether you're traveling or you're in hadar, whether you're a woman or a male, whether you have a reason or you don't have a reason. You don't even need a reason to wipe over the khuff; you don't have to be sick, you don't have to be traveling. Only the time frame differs; otherwise there is ijma', there is no controversy.

Okay, now that we've talked about no controversy: for example, no controversy would be over, mashaAllah, Texas boots. Okay, I have to say this in Texas. So you have the cowboy boots. MashaAllah, this is now khuff right there; this is the Texan khuff. So if you're wearing cowboy boots, and you had wudu when you wore them, by unanimous consensus you can wipe over. Now I think everybody's going to go buy cowboy boots to work, and now you're going to be real Texan when you go to work. You can do masah over the cowboy boots; no problem with something like that. Two conditions: number one, covering the ankle; number two, impermeable.

Okay, now we get to the controversy. What is the controversy? The controversy is: what if it's not a leather sock? As for not covering the ankle, no scholar says otherwise: if you're wearing a sock that goes below the ankle, you cannot do masah. No question, it has to cover the ankle; that's clear.

Now, what if it is not a leather sock? And the socks that we wear in our times, all of us, we wear nylon or cotton or polyester. These are the socks that we wear, and then we put our shoe over that. Now, this is where the controversy comes. Three of the madhhabs essentially do not allow wiping over permeable socks, and one of them allows it.

So the Hanafi madhhab: we have al-Haskafi in his al-Durr al-Mukhtar. He says that it is only allowed to wipe over coverings of the leg if they are very thick. He doesn't say leather; that's another common misconception. Some people say the Hanafis say it has to be leather. No, the Hanafis don't say it has to be leather. The Hanafis say it must be thick, such that you can walk one farsakh, which is like more than 5 kilometers, right, 3, 4, 5 miles. You can walk so many miles, one farsakh you can walk, and the sock will remain. So basically it's an independent shoe, almost. It's an independent shoe; that's what they are saying.

And al-Khalil, in his Mukhtasar, says that it is allowed for the male or the female, in travel and non-travel, that they may wipe over the socks if they are made out of leather. So a leather sock, meaning impermeable. And the same goes for the Shafi'is; Imam al-Nawawi also has a quote here, and others. So the three madhhabs say that it must be an impermeable sock.

The one madhhab that is left is which one? The Hanbali madhhab. And the Hanbali madhhab, out of the four madhhabs, was very clear that both the leather and the non-leather sock are allowed to do masah over, and this is something that they defended. Ibn Qudamah, in his famous book al-Mughni, basically mentions that anything that covers the ankle, and you can walk a little bit (not 5 kilometers, you can just walk), something that is an independent foot covering, which is basically any sock of our times, takes the ruling of the khuff, and you can do masah over it.

And Ibn Taymiyyah defended this position, and he goes: anything that covers the feet, even if it is very thin, as long as you call it a sock, a jawrab, then it is something that is permissible. And Ibn Hazm as well, famous scholar of the past, he also said this. And many of the modern scholars as well say this, as well as the Majlis al-Islami, Rabita: they have a fatwa on this, that it is completely permissible to do masah over cotton and polyester and wool, and it is not a condition that they be made out of leather. Even if the Shafi'is and Malikis and Hanafis said this, they said that it is not a condition.

And then what is their evidence? All of them, Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn Hazm, the Hanbali madhhab and many modern scholars, what is their evidence? The evidence is the authentic hadith in Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Musnad Imam Ahmad. Al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah said: I saw the Prophet ﷺ; he used to do masah 'ala al-jawrabayn wa al-na'layn, over his jawrab and his shoe. Now, in Arabic, khuff is a sock that is made out of leather, and jawrab is a sock that is made out of cloth. And in this hadith the word jawrab is mentioned. So he wiped over the jawrab. It's explicit in the hadith, and it is an authentic hadith.

Now the other three, they either said that, well, he meant a khuff, or they said, well, this is a jawrab that is impermeable and made out of this and that, and they kind of put all of these conditions on it. Nonetheless, Ibn Taymiyyah has a very long section in his Fatawa in which he says: the goal because of which Allah revealed the wiping over the sock was to make wudu easy, and for us to bring so many conditions that are not found in the Qur'an and Sunnah defeats the purpose of Allah gifting us. The point is that you make life easy. Because when you look at the hadith, the Prophet did not give any conditions at all.

These are later madhhabs, and we respect them. You know my position: I respect all the madhhabs. But when there is a diversity of opinion, if you wish to follow a particular madhhab, no problem from me. And that's why I'm giving you all the madhhabs; that's why I'm presenting the platter to you. If you want to be a Hanafi and you want to follow it, alhamdulillah, that's no problem. But if you ask me what is my humble opinion, humble Hanbali opinion... What is my humble Hanbali opinion? Not just because I am Hanbali overall, because you know I told you I'm overall Hanbali, but it is also my position that it is permissible for a person to follow another authority and say this position is the correct one. You're not fatwa shopping. You ask me a position, I give you my opinion.

It is my opinion, based on the evidences, that:

1. Number one, it is authentically narrated in multiple hadith that the Prophet ﷺ wiped over the jawrab, and jawrab is the word that means a sock made out of cloth.
2. Number two, the Prophet ﷺ did not put any condition.

It is true that most of the Arabs at that time wore leather socks, but that was the custom; that was the default. So he ﷺ usually wiped over the leather socks. Therefore that is the default, because that's what they had at that time. Even cloth was a scarcity, by the way, in that environment and whatnot. So cloth socks were not the default; leather socks were. But in that environment, our Prophet ﷺ, if it was only allowed for one type, he should have said masah is only allowed for khuff and not for jawrab. But he didn't. The Shari'ah came and allowed it; our Prophet ﷺ demonstrated it is allowed. So anyone who puts a condition, they need to be telling us where these conditions come from.

And with utmost respect to the other three madhhabs, the Hanbalis have a point here, and Ibn Taymiyyah says this: the goal is to make it easy, not to make it difficult. So this whole notion of "you have to walk 1000 yards, you have to make sure there's no hole the size of this and that"... Ibn al-Qayyim says: can you imagine any Sahabi did not have a hole in his sock? Can you imagine that? Everybody has holes in their socks. The sahabah were dirt poor; you don't think they had a hole? So to have a condition that the hole cannot be more than 2.7 cm, these things, with utmost respect... but you're making the religion... These conditions are coming, and it goes against the purpose of Allah revealing a concession to us.

So both Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim are somewhat defensive of the Hanbali position, and I find myself agreeing with this: **yes, you may do masah over any sock, as long as it is called a sock.** The Sunnah proves this explicitly, and the goals of the Shari'ah prove it implicitly. Is that clear? The Sunnah proves it explicitly, and the hadith is in Abu Dawud and Musnad Imam Ahmad, and the goals of the Shari'ah prove implicitly that it is allowed.

Now, having said that, the final point here: what is to be done if you are wearing a sock that covers the ankle? Because, as we said, if the sock does not cover the ankle, there is no discussion, end of story. You have to take it off and do washing of the feet. Now, what if it covers the ankle, and you put your shoe on top of the covered sock, but the shoe does not cover the ankle? So we have a number of scenarios.

First scenario: your shoe covers your ankle. In which case, clearly you can do masah over the shoe. You're wearing a boot, you're wearing anything that is a big covering, right, or these hiking boots that go all the way up: clearly you can do masah over that, there's no question. There's no ikhtilaf amongst the Hanbalis, and the other three would say only if the shoe is impermeable; we give that distinction, right? And by the way, most of the shoes, especially the hiking shoes, are impermeable; they don't want water to seep in. So according to those madhhabs it would be allowed. It doesn't have to be leather; the point, for the three madhhabs, is that water should not go in. The Hanbalis said even if water goes in, it doesn't matter; that's the point, you're allowed to do masah. So clearly, the first scenario: if the shoe goes above the ankle and it is impermeable, all three madhhabs allow it. Understand?

Now the controversy will come if the shoe goes beneath the ankle and the sock is above the ankle, which is our culture and custom in the Western world. Most of our fancy shoes are beneath the ankle, and the sock is above the ankle. And the Majlis al-Fiqhi of Europe and others have spoken about this in detail. And I always like to quote councils, because then nobody can say it's my personal opinion. Sometimes I will give you my personal one, but I try to avoid that, and I quote you respected scholars and whatnot, so that I get out of the picture.

And their position is, it's an interesting way, listen to this: in those days, most of these cloth socks were essentially wraparounds. In other words, they're not like ours, that you pull them up; it would be a strip, and you would wrap your feet, right, a type of band-aid. They would do it like that. So it's not one piece that you pull on; it is multi-layered, right? And the concept that we have of a thin sock to protect you from a shoe, that type of stuff wasn't there back then; this is something now.

So the Majma' said that in this case, really, if you look at it, as long as you had wudu... Because I mentioned this, you should all understand: if you don't have wudu, then this doesn't come in. You have to have wudu in the morning, meaning when you put your shoes and socks on. Not in the morning, but whenever you put your shoes and socks on, you need to have wudu.

Now, this Majma' said: if you look at it, this is essentially a multi-layered, one entity. Just imagine if you had a band-aid sock, and you took one layer above the ankle, then you went back down and did three or four layers on the foot itself. So the foot is thicker, band-aid wise, and above the ankle is one layer; it's considered one item. The point is it is covering; the hukm is the same. So they said that, given this modern circumstance, you're not going to find a classical position, because this is something new now, our style that we have. They said this qiyas is there, that this is one foot piece. So as long as you wore your sock and your shoe in the state of wudu, in one wudu (you understand this point: you wore your sock, and then you wore your shoes, and you had wudu), then you may do masah over the shoe, because you essentially wore it as one piece, and it can be counted as one piece.

Now, if you take your shoes off, according to this position, then you will have an issue. And if you don't have wudu when you place the shoe on, then you will have to take your shoe off and then do it with the sock. And this is one opinion, even in this issue.

Bottom line, Allah knows best, but Allah gave this concession, it's very clear, to make life easy. Allah says there is no difficulty in this religion. Allah says Allah wants to make things easy. Our Prophet ﷺ said Allah loves that the easy things He has given you, you should take advantage of them; don't reject them. And that's why, in the context of praying four versus two when you're traveling, you're not supposed to pray four, because Allah gifted you: you can pray two. And Allah wants you to accept His gift. When you're allowed to pray two, when you are actually musafir, you're supposed to pray two, as we all know; it is against the Sunnah to pray four. And in this context our Prophet ﷺ said: Allah loves that when He's given you a rukhsah, an easy thing, you take advantage of it.

So this is Ibn Taymiyyah's fatwa: that the whole concept of masah is a rukhsah from Allah, so why make it difficult? Make it easy. **As long as you have wudu and your footwear covers the ankle, then insha'Allah ta'ala you may do masah over that entire piece.** And therefore you do not even have to take your shoe off. Have the niyyah that you're going to do wudu in the morning, wear your socks and your shoes, and then for the rest of the day at work you can do masah, even over the shoe.

And if you don't remember whether you had wudu for the shoe or not (maybe you wore your socks, because it's cold these days, then you put your shoe on later), and if you forgot that, just to be on the safe side, you may take your feet out of the actual footwear, the shoe, and do masah over the socks.

But in my humble opinion, the Hanbali madhhab, Ibn Hazm, al-Tabari, many 'ulama of our times, and more and more 'ulama of our times, even many of the madhhabi 'ulama in our times, they are rethinking. They are looking at all of these explicit evidences. Many of the Shafi'i scholars of our times, by the way, allow masah over the jawrab. I was listening to some YouTube video of some of the Azhari scholars: even though they are Shafi'i, and technically their madhhab does not allow it, one of their great scholars was saying, "Look, the hadith is very clear," the al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah hadith, that the Prophet ﷺ wiped over the sock. And he said this hadith is very clear, and he's giving the fatwa, one of the main shaykhs of Azhar, and he's Shafi'i. He's saying the hadith is very clear.

So Allah knows best. It seems to be no problem whatsoever to do masah over any footwear whatsoever that constitutes footwear, and this is of the goals of the Shari'ah. And you may do your masah 24 hours when you are not traveling, and 76 hours, three days and nights, when you are traveling, insha'Allah.

So our brother is asking a good question that I didn't talk about: is masah done on the top or on the bottom? Ali ibn Abi Talib said, and the hadith is in Sunan Abu Dawud: if our religion were to be based upon what my logic and reason says, then I would have done masah on the bottom of my sock, my khuff, but I saw the Prophet ﷺ do masah on the top of the khuff. This hadith is in Abu Dawud, and Ali ibn Abi Talib said this: if the religion were to be based upon what I think is common sense, logic, rationality, then I would have thought masah should be done at the bottom, but I saw the Prophet do masah on the top.

And by the way, this shows that masah is symbolic. Masah is symbolic, because it's just a little bit of drops of water and you just rub on the top, even though we all know that when you're walking, it's the bottom that is going to be dusty and sandy and whatnot. This is Ibn Taymiyyah's point, by the way: that masah is a symbolic gift, like tayammum. So to add multiple conditions to tayammum defeats the purpose of tayammum; to add multiple conditions to masah defeats the purpose of masah. That's the point that Ibn Taymiyyah makes.
